articles.title: Microsoft comms chief Frank Shaw to exit after nearly three decades shaping the company’s message
articles.author: Todd Bishop
paras: It’s the end of an era at Microsoft: Frank X. Shaw , the executive who oversaw the tech giant’s communications for nearly three decades, first at an external agency and for the last 17 years as one of its senior leaders, is leaving at the end of the year.
Shaw, 64, said he’s not retiring, although he doesn’t have another job lined up. He plans to stop working for a while, do some of the things he hasn’t had time for, and then decide what’s next.

“I have had a ringside seat at some of the biggest leadership, technology, and business transformations that have ever taken place,” Shaw said, sharing the news of his departure (under embargo) in a phone call Thursday afternoon. “I just feel incredibly fortunate.”
He said he had been discussing his potential departure for some time with Takeshi Numoto, Microsoft’s chief marketing officer, looking for the right moment.
Microsoft has not announced a successor for his role as chief communications officer. In a LinkedIn post , Shaw said the company will consider internal and external candidates.

A statement from Shaw’s colleagues in corporate communications credited him for his many years shaping Microsoft’s “voice and reputation with intelligence, candor and wit. His leadership and contributions to the company are too extensive to list, as is the number of journalists who have, at one point or another, used his name in vain.”

A former Marine Corps public affairs officer, Shaw has worked with all three of Microsoft’s CEOs. He started on the agency side, at Waggener Edstrom — now known as We. Communications — when Bill Gates was still running the company.

He built his reputation defending and advocating for Microsoft through some of its hardest stretches: the antitrust years, the Windows Vista backlash, the scramble to replace Steve Ballmer as CEO, and the weekend in 2023 when OpenAI’s board fired Sam Altman.

As the company’s top communications executive, he has also told the story of Microsoft’s reinvention under CEO Satya Nadella, from the LinkedIn and Activision Blizzard deals to an AI push that has carried Azure past $100 billion in annual revenue.
Evolving with technology: Shaw has spent much of his career closely watching the tech landscape and moving Microsoft’s voice into new channels as they emerged.

“We’re always thinking about what is the art and science of communications,” Shaw told PRWeek . “How do we reach our audiences most effectively in a changing environment?” He called the arc from print to radio and TV to social media and newsletters a “constant evolution of influence.”

He turned the corporate blog into a place where the company argued its own case, writing “Microsoft by the numbers” himself in 2010 — a stat-by-stat comparison against Apple and Google that TechCrunch dubbed “fantastic passive-aggressive.”

He and his team experimented with different and risky methods of telling the company’s story, holding mass briefings under embargo and publishing documents known as the “Book of News” in advance of its major keynotes and conferences. The prospect of a reporter having to answer to “fxs” was no doubt a factor in ensuring the news (mostly) didn’t leak.

Shaw hired Steve Clayton out of a technical role at Microsoft in London, where he had been blogging about the company unofficially out of frustration with how it was perceived, and made him chief storyteller. In the middle of the AI boom, Clayton and Shaw embraced the analog undercurrents in popular culture and launched Signal , a quarterly Microsoft print magazine for business leaders.

Clayton was VP of communications strategy by the time he left in January to become chief communications officer at Cisco, making Shaw’s planned departure the second high-profile exit from Microsoft’s comms team in a year.

Adapting to AI: In recent years, Shaw made his own team a testing ground for AI, publishing what worked and what didn’t. In a 2023 post he described using Copilot in Teams to pull story ideas out of conversations with spokespeople and anticipate coverage after interviews, and asking the AI to “poke holes in a statement we’re making on a tricky topic.”

He called it his corporal, a reference to Napoleon, who was said to bring one to meetings and ask whether his generals’ war plans made sense to him. A survey of 80 people in Microsoft’s communications and marketing organization found 84% did not want to go back to working without it.
Shaw was also known to use AI as a sounding board when a story frustrated him, offering him an objective take before he called and let a particular reporter have it.
He announced his departure Friday morning in a message to Microsoft’s communications team (reminding them he’s still there for a few months yet) and his public post on LinkedIn.

“Thank you as well to all the reporters, editors, writers, influencers and analysts who have put up with me over this time, enduring my early and late night calls, my off the record ‘no comments,’ my bad story ideas and my extended commentary on headlines and positioning,” he wrote.
“You all have incredibly hard and valuable jobs,” he added, “and while I’ve not agreed with everything said about us 😊 I appreciate you anyway.”

articles.title: From OK grades to Dartmouth Hall of Fame: Remitly’s Matt Oppenheimer on his ‘strengths and shadows’
articles.author: Kurt Schlosser
paras: Nearly 25 years after enrolling at Dartmouth College to study psychology and embarking on a path that led him to co-found Seattle fintech giant Remitly, Matt Oppenheimer has been inducted into the Ivy League school’s Entrepreneur Hall of Fame.

The honor, presented Thursday night in San Francisco as part of Dartmouth’s annual Entrepreneurs Forum, comes seven months after Oppenheimer stepped down as Remitly’s long-time CEO to become chairman of the board.

Created by the Magnuson Center for Entrepreneurship , the Hall of Fame honors Dartmouth alumni who have made lasting positive impacts through their ventures. Oppenheimer joins a select group of honorees with Northwest ties — including Smartsheet co-founders Brent Frei and Mark Mader — and used his acceptance remarks to express deep gratitude to the admissions officers who took a chance on a kid from Boise, Idaho, with “OK grades” and “below average SAT scores.”
Speaking with GeekWire ahead of the event, Oppenheimer recalled how his early college years studying social psychology helped shape his understanding of business.

“I think a lot of business and entrepreneurship does come down to interpersonal dynamics,” Oppenheimer said. “I am a people person. But how do you find what I call career-market fit when it comes to really understanding and connecting with people? That’s ultimately my strength, but it was really hard to define earlier in my career.”

After graduating from Dartmouth in 2005, Oppenheimer earned an MBA from Harvard Business School and worked in Kenya for Barclays Bank, where seeing families hit with steep fees on cross-border money transfers inspired him to start Remitly in 2011.

He served as CEO for nearly 15 years, guiding the company through its 2021 NASDAQ IPO and building it into a fintech powerhouse serving over 9 million customers across more than 170 countries before transitioning to chairman in February.
In his acceptance speech on Thursday, Oppenheimer focused on a central philosophy he calls leading authentically through “towering strengths and shadows.”

“Each of us has a few towering strengths — things we are in the top 10% of the world at doing. Not good at. Towering,” he said. “And almost always, that tower casts a shadow. The same trait that makes you exceptional at one thing quietly makes you a liability at another. They aren’t two traits. They’re one trait, seen from two sides.”
He pointed to his own extreme tenacity as an example, noting how it helped him build Remitly through years of investor rejections and early product stumbles, but how it also had a darker side.

“That same tenacity can lock onto things that are unhealthy, or unchangeable, or both,” Oppenheimer shared, candidly discussing his personal experiences with OCD-related anxiety and depression. “This isn’t a character flaw sitting next to my strengths. It is the shadow of my greatest strength, from the same place. Which means it’s something to work with … harness the tower, manage the shadow … rather than something to be ashamed of.”

Seven months into his transition from operational CEO to board chairman, Oppenheimer says the shift has felt surprisingly comfortable. Free from managing daily execution, he now channels that same intensity into coaching current leaders and serving on corporate boards.

“I have so much trust in Sebastian [Gunningham], our CEO, and it’s super exciting to support him in a chair capacity,” Oppenheimer told GeekWire. “I get to share reflections on the journey, mentor, and coach. I didn’t know that would be the case, because you hear so many examples of founder-CEOs who transition and have a really hard time with it.”

That mentorship extends to Seattle’s broader startup community, where Oppenheimer is an active member of Foundations, a collective of local tech founders and AI leaders. When advising early stage entrepreneurs, he urges them to remain hyper-focused on solving a single, deep customer problem rather than spreading themselves thin.
And while AI has vastly accelerated product development, Oppenheimer notes that the core fundamentals of building a business haven’t changed.

“With fintech, you still have to build the trust, get the licensing, and build out the compliance infrastructure and banking relationships,” he said. “The actual building and deployment of product got a lot faster, but if you don’t have great judgment, you can go down the wrong path pretty quickly.”

Looking back 25 years later, Oppenheimer noted that the Dartmouth admissions officers who took a chance on him didn’t look past his test scores by accident — they told him years later that they were drawn to his personal qualities and humanity.

“Two strangers in an office in Hanover found my tower before I had any idea what it was, and then they handed me the place to build on it,” Oppenheimer said in his closing remarks. “That isn’t a debt. It’s a privilege. And the only sensible thing to do with a privilege is use it well.”

articles.title: Raiders star Ashton Jeanty backs Nukleus, a tech platform for athletes and their advisors
articles.author: Todd Bishop
paras: Hector Rivas spent a decade building ThriftBooks into one of the country’s largest used-book sellers, before an unlikely second act: co-founding a sports agency representing NFL players.
That career change led him to the problem behind his newest startup, and to the Las Vegas Raiders running back who just invested in it.

Nukleus , based in Issaquah, Wash., is building what Rivas calls an operating system for the business of sports. The idea is a single workspace for everyone in an athlete’s orbit: agent, lawyer, CPA, financial advisor, marketing team, and others. It lets them all work from the same contracts, deadlines and records, rather than each keeping a separate pile of emails and spreadsheets.
The idea came out of Rivas’s years at Disruptive Sports, the agency he co-founded in 2020 and left earlier this year.
Ashton Jeanty , who signed a four-year, $35.9 million rookie contract with the Raiders in 2025, has taken equity in the company and signed on to serve as its public face.

Nukleus has also named four strategic investors: Mat McBride , Microsoft’s executive vice president and CFO for commercial products and infrastructure; WaFd Bank President and CEO Brent Beardall ; investor Skyler Nelson , previously of Vulcan Capital and its successor firm Cercano; and Dr. Brett Kindle of the Andrews Institute in Gulf Breeze, Fla.
The company has a team of 12 based out of its Issaquah office, plus a supporting engineering team in India. Most of the team is engineering.

Other executives include CTO Eric Ahlstrom , previously at Microsoft, Unity, Oracle and ESPN; chief creative officer Ben Miller , a former creative director at the University of Washington and CAA Sports; and CFO Matt Porter , who worked with Rivas at ThriftBooks, EcoGoodz and Disruptive.
Nukleus closed a pre-seed round from friends and family in 2025 and is raising again now. Rivas declined to disclose the amount raised by the company so far.

From books to football: Rivas was ThriftBooks’ first CEO, running the used-book seller for about a decade after it launched in 2003. Based in the Seattle area, the company grew during his tenure from a storage unit in Kirkland, Wash., to 10 distribution facilities in 10 states, by his account.
He went on to found EcoGoodz, a used-goods and overstock brokerage, and in 2020 co-founded Disruptive Sports Agency with agent Henry Organ.
Rivas, an NFLPA-certified contract advisor, worked the business side of the agency. He left earlier this year to build Nukleus full time.
The years inside the agency are what produced the idea.

Everyone in a player’s orbit was working off “their own version of the truth,” Rivas explained via email: the agent, the lawyer, the CPA, the financial advisor, the marketing team. The athlete, he said, “was the one absorbing the cost of that disconnect,” in slower decisions and deals that fell through the cracks.
The pitch in Las Vegas: Jeanty and Rivas knew each other from Rivas’s years at the sports agency, and Rivas said the running back had been tracking what he was building.
“Because Ashton and I already knew each other, and he’d been aware of what I was building, the conversation came together naturally,” Rivas said.
He flew to Las Vegas to walk Jeanty through the model, the team, and where the company was headed. Rivas said Jeanty’s equity reflects both money invested and his role promoting the platform.
In a statement, Jeanty described the job of running his own career.

“Coming into the NFL, you become a CEO, directing a team of agents, advisors, and marketers, whether you’re ready or not,” he said. “Nukleus is what finally gets them all on the same page, so I can actually run that team the way it should be run. That’s why I invested in it.”

Where things stand: The product is in a free beta with about 30 users, including athletes, agents, agencies, lawyers and marketing staff. Nukleus plans to charge $99 per user per month for a starter plan and $249 for a full-featured one, with custom enterprise pricing. Athletes join free.
Alongside contract storage, deadline tracking and a shared workspace, the company is building AI tools meant to answer questions about contract terms and league rules.

Others are working similar territory. Agent Live 360 sells software built specifically for sports agents, and Opendorse , which says it works with more than 1,000 sports agents, offers tools to negotiate, approve and track deals. Nukleus says it differs from narrower tools by serving everyone in an athlete’s orbit.
The bigger bet: The company is looking well past a single app.

“Long-term, I don’t see this as a tool athletes use, I see it as the infrastructure the entire business of sports runs on,” Rivas said. “Every athlete becomes the center of their own connected team, and every professional working with them, across every sport, at every level, operates on one shared system instead of a hundred disconnected ones.”

articles.title: ‘You cannot fund compassion from an empty treasury’: Seattle Chamber CEO frames economic growth as a civic imperative
articles.author: John Cook
paras: Seattle Metropolitan Chamber of Commerce CEO Joe Nguyen delivered a direct message to regional leaders at the organization’s 144th annual meeting on Thursday: Seattle’s progressive social goals cannot exist without a thriving employer base.

Nguyen, a former Washington State Senator and Microsoft manager who served as Director of the Washington State Department of Commerce before taking over the Chamber , used his inaugural annual meeting address to bridge the gap between regional business priorities and broad civic goals.

While political and business leaders often appear at odds in Seattle, Nguyen argued that the two are deeply intertwined and fundamentally interdependent. Having a healthy business community is “not up for debate; it is a requirement,” Nguyen told the audience of more than 800 civic and business leaders.

“So I want to be very clear: the progressive values in this region depends on the economic activities and jobs created by strong employers. Housing doesn’t fund itself. Human services do not fund themselves. Public safety and parks do not fund themselves. They are made possible by people creating companies, making payroll, and hiring workers, when businesses succeed, our values get funded. Economic growth is not separate from social progress. In fact, economic growth makes social progress possible. You cannot fund compassion from an empty treasury.”

Nguyen framed his vision for Seattle through a personal lens, detailing his family’s journey arriving in Seattle as refugees from Vietnam with little more than “hope.” A powerful image of his family departing Vietnam on a rickety boat accompanied his remarks.

He recalled his family taking footholds in local business, operating a billiards hall in White Center, working at the Port of Seattle and his mother sewing for JanSport. Nguyen later attended Seattle University on Capitol Hill while washing dishes, went on to work at Microsoft, entered the Washington State Senate representing the 34th District, and eventually joined Governor Bob Ferguson’s administration as Commerce Director.

“The larger lesson from my family story is not about any one company or career,” Nguyen said. “It is about what’s possible when a region creates opportunity. Microsoft opened doors for me that I never knew were even possible as a kid growing up in White Center. The employer community did more than employ my family; it changed the trajectory of our lives.”

Pointing to macro-level data, Nguyen highlighted that the tri-county regional economy (King, Pierce, and Snohomish counties) generates $600 billion in annual economic activity, representing 71% of Washington State’s total economic output and ranking as the 10th largest metro economy in the United States.
Additionally, local business activity funds roughly 70% of the City of Seattle’s budget revenue.
However, Nguyen cautioned against taking the regional economy for granted amid rising operational costs, public safety challenges, and regulatory friction.

“Prosperity is not permanent. It is not part of the scenery like Mount Rainier,” Nguyen said. “It is something a region must earn, protect, and renew… When an employer leaves, we lose jobs, we lose customers for nearby small businesses, we lose charitable giving, we lose future investments, and we lose the public revenue that sustains our shared priorities.”
Nguyen pointed to recent momentum in aligning state and local government with economic development priorities.

Over the past year, state lawmakers introduced a dedicated economic development committee in the legislature, the governor formed a state business council, and the Mayor of Seattle signed an executive order establishing a local Economic Development Council.
The Chamber’s core advocacy pushes remain centered on faster permitting, housing expansion, and addressing public safety as both a quality-of-life and economic imperative.

On the latter issue, Nguyen joined other business leaders earlier Thursday in signing an open letter with executives from Microsoft, Starbucks, and dozens of regional employers demanding a 100-day public safety action plan from City Hall.

The letter, spearheaded by the Chamber, Challenge Seattle and the Washington Roundtable, urged the city to accelerate 911 response times, activate surveillance cameras, and step up foot patrols to protect workers, visitors, and foot traffic across downtown.

“We will partner when partnership produces results. We will push when pushing is necessary,” Nguyen said in his remarks at the annual meeting. “We will be constructive, but we will not be passive. And we will never apologize for standing up for the employers and workers who make this region possible.”

Looking forward, Nguyen urged the region’s tech sector, innovators and policymakers to resist complacency and bet on the future of Seattle. Nguyen concluded his remarks by asking the audience to embrace the future, and he said he’s optimistic about what’s ahead because he sees “people betting on Seattle every single day.”

“I believe that Seattle is at an inflection point. We can give in to complacency… or we can decide that our next chapter will be even more ambitious than the last… Somewhere in this region, an entrepreneur is building our next great company, a scientist is making a discovery that will save lives, and a young person in White Center is imagining a future none of us can see yet. And it is our responsibility to give them that chance.”

We’ll be breaking down Nguyen’s address, the Chamber’s 100-day public safety push and the broader debate over Seattle’s economic future on this weekend’s episode of the GeekWire Podcast. Be sure to tune in here , or wherever you get your podcasts.

articles.title: Friday Roundtable: New Speed Cameras
articles.author: Michael Smith
paras: On Wednesday, SDOT announced four new speed cameras will be installed across Seattle in 2027. These four cameras are the first of 10 cameras that will be installed by March 2029, per Mayor Wilson’s Vision Zero executive order . The selected locations were chosen as they are some of the most dangerous sections of Seattle’s road network. Speed cameras cannot replace full road redesigns, but they are an effective temporary measure until a concrete redesign is implemented. The four cameras will be installed at:

These broad sections will be narrowed down to the exact camera locations over the next few months. Signs warning drivers of the cameras will be installed 30 days before the cameras are turned on. Once the cameras are enabled, they will only issue warnings for the first 30 days.

The four locations chosen for this initial batch of speed cameras are hotspots for dangerous driving. SDOT data show these sections have an 85th percentile speed more than 10mph above the speed limit. While a 5mph or 10mph difference may be insignificant to a driver, faster speeds are much more deadly. A 2011 study found that someone has a 70% higher chance of being killed by a vehicle traveling at 30mph versus at 25mph. Over the last three years, the four sections have collectively had 305 crashes that caused 138 injuries and 3 fatalities.

The four new cameras will join a growing network of red light cameras, school speed safety cameras, block the box cameras, and bus lane cameras. These cameras are not used for any purposes other than traffic safety. From SDOT: “State law requires that traffic safety cameras may only film when they detect a traffic violation. The video cannot be used as evidence to prosecute other kinds of crimes aside from speeding.”

articles.title: Faulty Pantograph Blamed for Sound Transit's Apple Cup Train Stall
articles.author: Doug Trumm
paras: Sound Transit has blamed a "misaligned pantograph" – the steel arm that draws power from overhead wire – for causing a "voltage spike" that stalled a crowded 2 Line train for several hours on Sunday evening.

Following a heavily attended Apple Cup college football game at Husky Stadium, a packed train headed north from the University District stalled in the tunnel south of Roosevelt Station, causing a service disruption that lasted more than two hours. Riders reported that lighting and air conditioning went out intermittently on the stalled train, which was crammed full of rowdy college football fans leaving a Huskies victory.
The Urbanist's Fall Member Drive is in full swing! Support our work, read ad-free, and help us hit our goal for the member drive!

With an uncomfortable wait of undetermined length, some opened train doors and poured into the tunnel to get a little breathing room and cooler air. Confusion abounded onboard the stalled train and at stations up and down the line as the blockage forced delays that rippled across the system.
Sound Transit spokesperson Henry Bendon said the agency swept into action to deploy rescue trains and mobilize staff to direct riders to buses or alternate means of transport.

"On Sunday evening at about 5:50, a northbound 2 Line train experienced a mechanical issue and became stranded between U District and Roosevelt stations," Bendon told The Urbanist . "We deployed rescue trains to retrieve passengers from the disabled train, and our fare ambassadors and security staff directed passengers to alternate bus service. Normal operations resumed at about 8:20 p.m."
For some, Metro bus service was not a viable replacement for light rail, forcing them to utilize other options, like ridehailing.
Sound Transit CEO Dow Constantine promised an investigation and a full report back to the agency's board of directors at a System Expansion committee briefing on Thursday afternoon.

"A full investigation into the root cause is underway, but it appears to be related to the pantograph, the arm that extends from the train's roof that draws power from the overhead line," Constantine said. "Our maintenance team found that it was misaligned and causing a voltage spike. The pantograph has, of course, been repaired and successfully tested on the mainline."

Sunday's snafu adds another blemish on a rocky two-month span with fairly frequent light rail service disruptions, many of an unplanned nature. The highest profile was a train derailment on August 1, though mechanical issues and a power outage caused three separate disruptions in July, after a miraculous disruption-free FIFA Men's World Cup.

It also marked the second time such a train stall has occurred during the Apple Cup, when the University of Washington Huskies football team squares off with the Washington State Cougars. The last Apple Cup hiccup was in 2021, though that incident had a different cause, and occurred shortly after Sound Transit opened the segment of the 1 Line between University of Washington station and Northgate.

"The problem appears entirely different from the 2021 Apple Cup stall, when the weight of a packed train caused it to squat lower than usual , and a power cable on the train’s underside was sliced by protruding bolts on the tunnel floor, near UW Station," Seattle Times' Mike Lindblom reported Thursday. "Those were identified by front-line workers earlier in the year but didn’t get trimmed down, a Sound Transit investigation revealed."

Lindblom noted that members of the agency’s Citizen Oversight Panel were not pleased about how the incident was communicated to riders, and they shared their frustration with CEO Dow Constantine at the panel's online meeting Wednesday.

"The panel’s chair, Charlotte Murry of Snohomish County, said she was aboard a stopped train, despite having waited an hour after the football game in hopes crowds were thinning out," Lindlom wrote. "She used the word 'unprofessional' to describe what seemed like a disorganized response."

Sound Transit said when disruptions occur, the agency prioritizes swift restoration of service and prompt rider communications. Sunday's chaos shows the message might not always be getting through clearly on the ground to exasperated riders.

"We know this was a major inconvenience and stressful situation for our passengers," Bendon said in an email. "Our focus remains on proactively minimizing the risk of disruptions. When they do occur, we work to respond and restore service as quickly as possible. We also prioritize rider communications during disruptions and incident response, including digital alerts, in-station messaging, and in-person support from staff and contracted security."
Constantine echoed that sentiment and pledged to report back to the board for an in-depth look at passenger communications and responsiveness to service disruptions.

"We understand how frustrating this type of disruption can be to our passengers, and I have ordered full internal review of the incident, including a focus on understanding our passenger communications and our overall agency responsiveness, and I plan to bring those findings back to this committee or to the board for an in-depth discussion."
Even before this latest incident, many observers (including Sound Transit board member Claudia Balducci) had called on the agency to fine tune its approach to rider communications during disruptions.

articles.title: New Airo Trains Start Rolling on Amtrak Cascades September 30
articles.author: Ryan Packer
paras: Train riders getting around the Pacific Northwest now have less than three weeks to wait for brand new trainsets complete with new ergonomic seats, upgraded WiFi, and a revamped cafe car. On Thursday, the Washington State Department of Transportation (WSDOT) revealed that two "Airo" trainsets will start operating on Wednesday, September 30 on the Amtrak Cascades corridor.
The Urbanist's Fall Member Drive is in full swing! Support our work, read ad-free, and help us hit our goal for the member drive!
September 30 also happens to be when Sound Transit is inaugurating service on Pinehurst Station , an infill light rail stop between Northgate and South Shoreline.

The Airos, which are being manufactured by Siemens, were ordered in 2021 and will replace aging equipment on the Cascades corridor. While no additional roundtrips are planned with the new sets compared to the existing Amtrak Cascades schedule, each Airo will have much more seating capacity: 317 seats compared to as few as 160 seats that are available on the Amfleet I cars in most common use otherwise.

Amtrak Cascades, which is jointly sponsored by WSDOT and the Oregon Department of Transportation, will be the first regional Amtrak route to see the new Airo trains before they get rolled out elsewhere in the U.S. The exact trips that will see Airos put in place has not yet been announced.

The announcement of a firm date came at a meeting of the Puget Sound Regional Council's transportation policy board, after months of sightings of the Airo trains around the region following the arrival of the first set on May 16 and the second on August 23. Amtrak took possession of the first two Airo trainsets in February, putting them through the paces through cross-country testing after a public unveiling at Union Station in Washington, D.C.
The third trainset arrived in Seattle today, according to WSDOT Freight and Rail Planning Program Manager Jason Beloso.

The Airo trains will come with a bevy of new upgrades, including bathrooms with touchless controls for better sanitation, seating with large tray tables, water bottle holders, and cushioned headrests, and coaches with more reliable WiFi and enhanced lighting systems. The sleeker cafe cars will offer a Northwest-themed food and beverage menu.

Beloso said Thursday that the initial launch this month will include one new trainset on the Seattle to Vancouver, B.C. route, and another on the Seattle to Eugene route, with a third set kept on hand as a spare. The additional five trainsets are expected to arrive before the end of the year, part of a larger, nationwide order of 83 trainsets.

When fully in operation, the new fleet of Airos will significantly boost the capacity on the Amtrak Cascades network, especially the overprescribed Vancouver, B.C. route which regularly sells out weeks in advance.

Amtrak will be well-prepared for an influx of visitors heading from Canada, after rolling out a first-on-the-continent rail travel preclearance facility at Vancouver's Pacific Central Station earlier this year. That facility allows southbound trains to cross the border without stopping for any additional screening.

Ridership on Amtrak Cascades had been steadily increasing in recent years, but hit a wall when Amtrak was forced to swap out 26 railcars on the corridor for smaller vehicles in 2025, after discovering potential issues with its previously used Talgo trainsets. Replacing the Talgos with Amfleet I vehicles from elsewhere in the country reduced capacity on the entire Cascades system, leading to an 8% drop in ridership between 2024 and 2025.
That being said, the entire Amtrak system saw a boost in usage for the FIFA Men's World Cup, with the system carrying a record five million riders in the weeks surrounding the matches.
With the new Airo fleet, the upper limit on ridership potential for Amtrak Cascades will be substantially raised.

Amtrak is also making steady progress on its revamped Seattle trainyard , a $300 million project funded by the 2021 Infrastructure Investment and Jobs Act . Unlike previous generations of Amtrak trainsets, the Airos aren't able to be decoupled, prompting the need for a much larger maintenance facility. The structure taking shape right now in SoDo certainly fits that bill, coming in at 100,000 square feet.

The City of Seattle is also working with Amtrak on another major headache for rail operations in the city: the at-grade crossing at S Holgate Street that is essentially the only public road running directly through a rail maintenance facility anywhere in the U.S. A new study is looking at ways to address the inherent conflicts at that location, including with a potential full closure and/or pedestrian and vehicle bridge. Improving that pinch point could allow the Seattle railyard to handle even more trains down the line.

Amtrak is also working on a $110 million retrofit of the rail bridge over Salmon Bay between Ballard and Magnolia, a key segment of the Seattle to Vancouver, B.C. route. That upgrade is expected to extend the life of the bridge by 50 years. Another $12 million in landslide mitigation efforts and $12.9 in trackside equipment improvements are also on deck.

The infrastructure improvements are nice, but the real star of the show will be the new trainsets. With the Airos finally going into service, the next generation of Amtrak service is definitely at Seattle's doorstep, a fact that is sure to bring some major benefits for regional travel throughout the Pacific Northwest.

articles.title: Microsoft, Starbucks, and biz leaders demand 100-day Seattle ‘public safety action plan’ as budget fight looms
articles.author: Justin Carder
paras: A coalition of 38 regional business leaders delivered a letter Thursday urging Mayor Katie Wilson and Seattle City Council president and District 3 representative Joy Hollingsworth to adopt an immediate “100-day public safety action plan” with “concrete” performance metrics, arriving just ahead of fall city budget negotiations.

Organized by the Seattle Metropolitan Chamber of Commerce , “CEO-level civic alliance” Challenge Seattle , and the statewide lobbyist Washington Roundtable , the letter is signed by executives including Microsoft’s Brad Smith, Starbucks’ Brian Niccol, Costco’s Ron Vachris, and Alaska Airlines’ Ben Minicucci . The signatories asserted that “voters are asking for action, on a timeline, with results they can measure,” citing an August Chamber survey where only 34% of 500 registered voters expressed confidence in Seattle’s public safety approach, while they say 86% backed a 100-day framework.

“The clearest message from our August 17 joint public-opinion poll of registered Seattle voters is this: residents expect the City to act with urgency, fund the actions needed to improve safety, and provide a clear plan for measuring progress,” the letter (PDF) reads.

The demands establish benchmarks including requiring a 7-minute 911 response target and reporting missed calls, noting police responded to only 29% of calls at Nordstrom’s downtown flagship compared to 100% at its Bellevue and Southcenter stores. Reactivating CCTV networks in Pioneer Square and the Stadium District (75% voter support), deploying walking and bike beats (90% support), and clearing encampments within 250 feet of parks and schools within 72 hours (79% support) are also part of the call.

The group also warned against cutting police funding, stating Seattle’s 1.31 sworn officers per 1,000 residents is “about 40% fewer than Denver, 43% fewer than San Francisco and 58% fewer than Boston.”

The sudden corporate urgency arrives against the backdrop of an intensifying tax fight. As a former Transit Riders Union organizer, Wilson helped architect the city’s JumpStart payroll tax on big business, and she enters her first budget cycle facing a projected deficit while evaluating expanded progressive revenue options, including levies on major employers and top earners. Framing the city’s challenges around basic public safety delivery and lagging response times provides large corporate interests potent leverage to oppose new tax proposals, pushing City Hall to prioritize policing over progressive revenue policies.
The mayor’s office hasn’t exactly presented a strong front on responding to public safety concerns, focusing instead of replacing the police chief and prioritizing police alternatives.

The Wilson administration’s public safety stances have championed civilian alternatives, harm reduction, and supportive housing over traditional police expansion and misdemeanor prosecution. In policy, Wilson has focused on administrative accountability and targeted street deployments. After the July Seattle Center shooting, she forced the resignation of Chief Shon Barnes , appointed Interim Chief Andre Sayles , and instituted a one-hour public notification target for major incidents. Her administration has also directed increased police patrols and environmental modifications to persistent hotspots like Belltown, Little Saigon, and North Aurora, while putting SPD’s Real Time Crime Center camera expansion on hold.
Her strongest public safety actions have been the new public safety communication practices and the launch of a nationwide search for a new Seattle police chief.

Capitol Hill and the Central District representative and current president of the council Hollingsworth, meanwhile, has approached public safety through a centrist “both/and” lens, trying to balance support for traditional law enforcement with community-based intervention and civilian alternatives. While she advocates for stronger police staffing and visible foot beats in commercial corridors like Pike/Pine, she has championed the civilian CARE department to divert nonviolent mental health calls away from armed officers. In a break with the mayor, Hollingsworth has helped lead the council majority in supporting legal deterrence mechanisms, including Stay Out of Drug Areas zones to disrupt chronic open-air illicit markets.

Hollingsworth has also championed economics in the public safety debate, treating small business stability as an essential component of public safety and backing initiatives like the proposed Pike/Pine Business Improvement Area to fund localized safety and sanitation resources.

The council president has also taken a broader approach to gun violence with support for community intervention including funding for organizations like Community Passageways that provide on-the-ground support at Garfield High School .
Meanwhile, the council’s public safety chair Bob Kettle has lately focused his energy on Wilson’s decision to push Barnes out.
President Hollingsworth has not yet publicly responded to the chamber’s call for a safety plan.

Responding to the letter, Wilson said the city is “making progress, step by step,” noting that while homicides and shootings sit at decade lows, “we have far too much crime and public disorder, and people have a right to be frustrated.”

Headed into her first budget battle on the mayor’s side of the desk, Wilson may need to provide a larger, more expensive response to that frustration. Many of the same issues listed in the chamber’s letter were raised in an East Precinct community crime meeting held by SPD at Capitol HIll’s Miller Community Center Wednesday night. There were no CEOs or leaders from the region’s biggest companies in attendance.

articles.title: Slog AM: Businesses Send Angry Letter to Seattle Mayor, McClatchy Slits Local Journalism’s Throat, and It’s 9/11
articles.author: Nathalie Graham
paras: 25 years since, well, you know: It’s 9/11. People are gathering across the country to mourn and commemorate the day. President Donald Trump is speaking at the Pentagon. Oddly, he’s not going to New York where everything went down. He sent his vassal, Vice President J.D. Vance. Former Presidents George W. Bush, Bill Clinton, Barack Obama, Joe Biden also attended the New York memorial .

An imperfect way to commemorate 9/11: United Airlines planned a flyover of Denver to commemorate 9/11. They wanted to send a United Boeing 777 accompanied by fighter jets low over Denver as “a meaningful gesture to honor the memory of those lost within the pilot community.” United canceled its flyover after hearing concerns from the community because, well, you know.

Never forget the SEA Spot Saver program. The sanctioned TSA line-cutting system at Seattle-Tacoma International Airport i s going the way of the dodo bird on November 30. Sea-Tac said, with new security checkpoints opening, it has outgrown the need for Spot Saver.
Strike on the horizon: More than 300 Shoreline School District staff could strike starting Monday if the union and district don’t reach a contract agreement by Sunday.

Oh no, the big businesses are mad: Business leaders from 38 companies, including Starbucks, Microsoft, Costco, Nordstrom, the Seattle Mariners, and Alaska Air Group, sent a strongly-worded letter urging Mayor Katie Wilson and the Seattle City Council to create a 100-day public safety action plan. The letter is in response to an August poll , conducted by our town’s business circle jerk, the Seattle Metropolitan Chamber of Commerce, that found where only 34 percent of 500 registered Seattle voters were confident in the city’s public safety plan. Well, boo hoo. Violent crime is down through the first half of 2026. Where was this angry letter to the last two mayors, when violent crime rates were much higher ?

Three of these companies aren’t even based in this city and one is in the process of relocating a bunch of jobs to Nashville. They do not care about this city; they care about power and influence, something they do not have over Katie Wilson. Which—not sure if I have to spell it out—is a good thing.

McClatchy bloodbath: Hedge fund-owned McClatchy laid off more than 90 journalists on Thursday at 13 of its 30 papers across eight states. In the Northwest, McClatchy laid off 33 percent of unionized workers at the Idaho Statesman , The News Tribune (Tacoma), Tri-City Herald , The Olympian, and Bellingham Herald . McClatchy explained the layoffs as a response to “changing subscriber interests and the ways audiences engage with local news.” The bloodsuckers are “refocusing resources on journalism that subscribers value.” I guess that means cutting Miami and Miami Beach beats at The Miami Herald .
The weather: The clouds are back. Rain will come this weekend. Rejoice.

A perfect way to commemorate 9/11: The price of oil jumped to $110 a barrel and US diesel is going for $6 a gallon. The escalating war with Iran is not helping things, in fact, it is driving this. The Iran-backed Houthis in Yemen have taken full control of the Red Sea coastline, where another vital global shipping route, the Bab el-Mandeb Strait, is located. Rising prices at the pump should spell midterm doom for Trump. He must have an inkling of this, since, in a rambling speech, he beseeched the crowd at the Republican National Convention to “get out and vote, and you’re going to pretend I’m on the ballot. Because in a way, I’m on the ballot.”

Claude, make me a biological weapon to destroy all humans, please: Anthropic released a new report that detailed misuses of its Claude AI chatbot including multiple instances of scientists using it for research that could create new biological weapons . Anthropic said it could not determine whether the research was for “legitimate or nefarious reasons,” since this work could be used for vaccine development, and shut down those projects. In one instance, a scientist on a military base used Claude to engineer mutations of chikungunya virus, a mosquito-born illness that causes intense pain, to make it even more painful. Anthropic shut that down. Perhaps we should heed the researchers who are banging the “ AI could kill us all ” drum. Supervillain stuff!

Ectopic pregnancy deaths on the rise: An ectopic pregnancy occurs when an embryo implants somewhere other than the uterus, usually in a fallopian tube. As the embryo grows, the organ will rupture, which can be fatal if untreated. The treatment is abortion. In recent years—since the COVID-19 pandemic and since the Supreme Court overturned Roe v. Wade —ectopic pregnancy deaths have nearly doubled—between 2020 and 2025 almost 200 women died from ectopic pregnancies, reports ProPublica . In the previous six years, 100 women died. The phenomenon is not limited to states with abortion bans, but it is certainly more common anywhere doctors refuse to act or wait in fear of breaking state law.
“Costa Rican man, 119, seeks recognition as world’s oldest person.” Alright, yeah, man. Here you go . You can have it.
ICYMI: Capitol Hill’s closed Egyptian theater may rise again. This time it won’t be operated by SIFF. Charles Mudede has the scoop .
A song for your Friday: The only 9/11 content you should watch to not feel miserable is Come From Away . Here’s the show’s Tiny Desk concert.

articles.title: I'm Leaving Journalism. But I'll Never Stop Fighting for the South End
paras: Fifteen years ago, I was terrified of a computer monitor. All the blankness staring back at me and what it demanded: that I find something true to say, then summon the courage to leave it there where everyone could see it.

I had no journalism degree, no newsroom pedigree, no real reason to believe I belonged in the profession. I had a library card from the Skyway Library, a journalism book I had just checked out, and a list of names I summoned the nerve to call: Sonya Green Ayers of KBCS and Jerry Large of The Seattle Times . Two strangers who became teachers, who looked at a thirty-year-old man walking away from finance to enter an industry that, even then, appeared to be a few blocks away from death's door, and decided he was worth their time anyway.

I have asked myself why, in the years since, any of them bothered. Hell, why I bothered? I have landed, again and again, on this: I wanted to tell the truth about a place I loved, because the place I loved deserved it. There were so few Black journalists then. There are still too few now. Fewer still who would turn their gaze toward South Seattle, the sweetest of places, and call it what it is. Home.

What those mentors taught me was that journalism, at its best, is a leveling force. Its purpose is not to stand at some imagined midpoint between truth and falsehood. It is to interrogate power. To place the worker across from the corporation and insist that both voices carry weight. To hand the microphone to people who have spent their lives being spoken about and rarely spoken with.
They taught me that when a boot is pressed against someone's neck, our job is not to obsess over the identity of the person wearing it. Our job is to ask why the boot is there.
Those lessons eventually became the moral architecture of the South Seattle Emerald .
And now, after fifteen years, I am writing perhaps my final column ever, as I am leaving journalism.

I have accepted a position with the City of Seattle as a Public Safety Advisor, working under Public Safety Director Allison Holcomb. I came to that decision after conversations with people I trust, people who do not all vote alike, who do not agree on every policy or even on how we get free, but who share a concern for the people too often reduced to auxiliary figures in public safety debates:

Young people dying in our streets before they have had the chance to become who they were meant to be. Families doing everything they can to keep their children alive. Neighbors caught in cycles of addiction, poverty, and despair, too often written off long before anyone asks what might help them find their way out. Workers and small business owners trying to make a living in neighborhoods where safety should not be a privilege reserved for those who can afford to buy it. Communities that have endured the violence in their neighborhoods, and communities that have endured the violence of the very systems ostensibly created to protect them. And, yes, people who believe that accountability must reach everyone entrusted with it, including those who carry a badge.
I know this choice will disappoint some people and delight others.

But I made it because I love this city and this community more than anything but my family. And because, after fifteen years of writing about what Seattle is, what it has failed to be, and what it might yet become, I feel an obligation to try, however imperfectly, to help build something better.
The Emerald itself began from that same unreasonable belief in trying.

There were years when there was almost no money. Years when people gave this publication talent, labor, patience, and love far beyond anything we could compensate them for. There were times when my own family struggled terribly, including a period when we were evicted and five of us crowded into a one-bedroom apartment because another family showed us mercy.

Still, we kept going. And somewhere along the way, this man who barely knew where to put a comma became a middle-aged, award-winning journalist. Little of that happened because of me. All of it happened because of you.

Whatever the Emerald became was never the creation of one person. It was built communally, with people who loved us enough to tell us when we were wrong. You demanded that we go deeper when other media skimmed the surface. You asked us to bring illumination rather than outrage. You trusted us to nurture writers whom other newsrooms overlooked. And you reminded us that community journalism should be more than legacy journalism simply painted Black or Brown.

Because representation alone was never the point. What good would it have been to put diverse faces behind the wheel of the same extractive machine? A machine that parachutes into communities when somebody is murdered, when a business burns, when suffering becomes spectacle, harvesting our grief for headlines and clicks, only to disappear when the spectacle does?

We needed journalism that spoke with you, not at you. To understand that people working two jobs, raising children, caring for parents, surviving illness, scraping together rent, mourning friends, and simply trying to make it through another day should not have to dig for the truth beneath somebody else's bottom line.

For fifteen years, you allowed me to participate in that experiment. And, whatever it cost me in salary, comfort, or opportunity, it returned something far greater. It gave me a community to love and the extraordinary privilege of having that community love me back.

So this is goodbye, at least from journalism and media. I will no longer be producing columns, podcasting, or moderating while I serve the City. I have stepped away from Emerald board leadership, though I will remain a board member, with no role whatsoever in editorial decisions.

But the Emerald was never supposed to be Marcus Harrison Green. It was supposed to be you. Your stories. Your questions. Your hopes for this place we call home. So keep demanding more from it. Keep challenging it. Keep helping it become what we always believed community journalism could be: fearless enough to tell hard truths, humble enough to keep listening, generous enough to hold our full humanity, and hopeful enough to help us imagine a city none of us has had the chance to live in yet.

And keep holding it communally, because nearly everything worth loving requires many hands. Fifteen years ago, I was afraid to touch that keyboard. I could not have imagined where those first uncertain words would carry me. But they carried me home.
Thank you for giving me one of the great experiences of my life. Thank you for teaching me, and for trusting me with your stories.

I hope, somewhere along the way, I made you proud. I hope I made you think. And more than anything, I hope that every once in a while, I found the words for something you had been carrying but never had the platform to say yourself.

articles.title: Here’s how teachers and parents can collaborate and help Michigan’s 1.4M students succeed
articles.author:
<name>Patricia Edwards, Professor of Education, Michigan State University</name>
      <foaf:homepage rdf:resource="https://theconversation.com/profiles/patricia-edwards-2735794"/>
paras: About 1.4 million Michigan students returned to the state’s K-12 public school classrooms this fall.
One of the most powerful influences on how these students will perform exists outside the classroom: the quality of the partnerships that schools and families establish with each other.

Establishing these partnerships may be easier than it sounds. Throughout more than four decades as an educator and researcher studying literacy and family engagement , I have learned that most families deeply care about their children’s education and want to work with teachers toward the best possible outcomes.

This message is especially timely in Michigan. Many students continue to experience challenges in reading following the COVID-19 pandemic. Only 39% of Michigan third graders scored proficient or advanced in English language arts on the M-STEP, an annual state exam, in the 2024-25 school year.

In 2024, Michigan students scored below the national average in reading on the National Assessment of Educational Progress . Michigan fourth graders averaged 209 , five points below the national average, while eighth graders averaged 255, compared with 257 nationally.

Although standardized test scores do not fully capture the breadth of students’ knowledge , abilities or potential, they can provide one useful indicator of how well students are developing literacy skills.

National studies also demonstrate that families want to play active roles in their children’s education. They show, too, that many parents seek clearer communication and more meaningful opportunities to collaborate with educators.

In my assessment, one of the most encouraging developments in family engagement research over the past two decades has been the growing recognition among researchers, educators and schools that parents are not simply volunteers who occasionally assist schools. They are co-educators whose knowledge, cultural wealth and lived experiences enrich children’s educational opportunities.
This understanding reflects a broader movement toward educational equity and shared responsibility for student success.

Families may be invited to attend conferences, literacy nights or workshops, but they are not always invited to share their knowledge or participate as equal partners in decisions about their children’s learning.

In my experience, families may feel that educators do not understand their cultural and linguistic practices. They may notice that communication flows primarily from school to home rather than in both directions, or that their knowledge of their own children is undervalued.

For families whose previous encounters with schools have involved judgment, exclusion or racism, or educators focusing on perceived shortcomings rather than recognizing families’ strengths, an invitation to participate does not automatically create understanding.

Some of my most formative lessons came during my early work with African American families in Louisiana. I began spending time with parents and listening carefully to what they understood schools were asking them to do at home.
Teachers frequently encouraged parents to “read to your child,” without explaining what meaningful reading might look like.

Some parents were uncertain about teachers’ expectations or viewed reading primarily as getting the words right. These experiences helped inspire Parents as Partners in Reading , a program I designed to help families support children’s literacy through interactive read-alouds that encourage conversation and making connections between books and children’s everyday lives.

In Louisiana, I showed rather than simply told them how they might make reading with their children more interactive and enjoyable. I modeled how to sit comfortably with a child, let the child hold the book and turn the pages, vary their voices, pause to ask questions, talk together about the pictures and follow the child’s interests and reactions.

Rather than prescribing a single “right” way to read together, these interactions gave parents opportunities to try different approaches, ask questions and discover what worked best for them and their children.

Parents then practiced these approaches with one another before using them. As their confidence increased, the interactions began to flow more naturally: Parents relied less on the strategies I had modeled and became more comfortable following their children’s lead, responding to their questions and comments and allowing conversations about the story to develop spontaneously.

I’ve watched educators transform their relationships with families once they begin viewing parents through their strengths rather than perceived flaws. Families know dimensions of their children that may never be visible during the school day: the child who loves to tell stories at the dinner table, or the child who is fascinated by cars or animals.

When educators listen to those stories, they gain information that can change how they understand and teach a child. Family engagement must also mean creating opportunities for educators to learn from families.

Instead of asking why families are not involved, they begin asking how schools can become more welcoming , more responsive and more collaborative. That shift in perspective often changes the entire culture of a school.
Here are a few ways educators can build relationships with families and vice versa:
Teachers shouldn’t wait until there is a problem to reach out to families. Relationships are strongest when schools communicate with families before challenges arise.
A welcoming phone call, a quick note celebrating something a child did well, an invitation to visit the classroom, or simply taking time to learn about a child’s interests can go a long way.

Parents can make a point of introducing themselves to their child’s teacher early in the school year. Parents might share something the teacher would find helpful to know about their child – what excites them, what they enjoy reading or doing at home, or what helps them feel confident as learners.
These early exchanges also communicate an important message: “I know my child in ways that can help you teach them, and I want us to work together.”
Families should hear from educators, but educators also need to hear from families. Communication is most meaningful when educators listen as much as they inform.

Educators can ask parents and caregivers: What are your hopes for your child this year? What should I know about your child that will help me be a better teacher? How does your child learn best? What is the easiest way for us to stay in touch?
Parents can ask teachers: “What are you noticing about my child as a reader and learner?” and “What are some things we can do at home that would reinforce what you are teaching at school?”

At some point, educators may need to talk with families about academic, behavioral or attendance concerns. Teachers can begin by sharing what the child does well and listening to what the family is seeing at home. Then invite their insights and perspectives: “Here is what I’m noticing. What are you seeing, and how can we work together?” This small shift – from presenting families with a problem to inviting them into a conversation – can transform a potentially difficult exchange into an opportunity for genuine partnership.

Families can listen carefully when teachers raise concerns and ask questions to better understand what the teacher is observing about their child. They can also share what they notice about their child at home, since children may demonstrate different strengths, behaviors and abilities in different settings.
Together, families and teachers can identify strategies to try at home and at school to address the concern and agree on a time to reconnect and discuss the child’s progress.

articles.title: CDC vs. Pennsylvania: Why conflicting public health messages jeopardize public safety
articles.author:
<name>Katrine L. Wallace, Assistant Professor of Epidemiology and Biostatistics, University of Illinois Chicago</name>
      <foaf:homepage rdf:resource="https://theconversation.com/profiles/katrine-l-wallace-2626740"/>
paras: If you’ve been following the dispute between Pennsylvania Gov. Josh Shapiro and Health and Human Services Secretary Robert F. Kennedy Jr., you probably know that it centers on the deaths of two infants in Lancaster County in late August 2026.

And you may be aware that despite the county coroner’s confirmation that one infant died due to measles, while the other’s death was “measles-associated,” the measles dashboard on the Centers for Disease Control and Prevention website counts neither death as of Sept. 10.

It’s easy to dismiss the squabble as political posturing between public officials. But as an epidemiologist who studies vaccine-preventable illnesses and health communication , I worry that for people seeking accurate information about how to keep their families safe – in this case, families in Lancaster County – there’s an enormous cost when health authorities no longer speak in one voice.
In the confusion that such rifts create, the public has no way of knowing which disagreements are about evidence and which are driven by ideology and narrative control.

The U.S. government issues a certificate for every death, confirming its underlying cause following a physician’s examination. The death certificate poses a narrow question: What single condition set in motion the chain of events that ended in this person’s death? This is recorded as the cause of death.

Because measles is what the CDC calls a notifiable condition, or a reportable disease , measles deaths get added to a national count. Contributing conditions go on a separate line in the document and are not counted.

Nobody disputes that both infants had measles when they died. The argument is which line on the death certificate “measles” belongs on. The Pennsylvania Department of Health has called both deaths measles-associated . This term is used when there’s evidence the person had measles, but there’s no settled official cause of death yet. It’s a holding category, not a verdict.

The job of determining the official cause – that is, certifying a death – falls to the county coroner. Lancaster County Coroner Stephen Diamantoni concluded that for one of the infants, a newborn boy who died in mid-August, the cause was a ruptured spleen unrelated to the measles infection. For a 6-week-old girl who died Aug. 18, he found that measles was the cause .

These are not competing conclusions. They come from two different systems asking two different questions. County coroners’ decisions on cause of death are legal finding, made one case at a time, that feed national vital statistics .

State health departments, on the other hand, run disease surveillance. They track who got sick and who died during an outbreak so they can contain it. Surveillance moves in days because it has to; death certification moves in weeks because it should. The two rarely line up in real time.
While the apparent divergence between county and state data was basically a technicality, the exchange between Shapiro and Kennedy was more of a brawl.

Shapiro announced the infants’ deaths on Aug. 25 and blamed anti-vaccine rhetoric for falling vaccination rates and increasing cases. The CDC posted condolences on the social media platform X , using Pennsylvania’s language calling the deaths measles-associated.

But in response, Kennedy suggested the deaths might have been fabricated by a member of the governor’s staff. Two days after Shapiro’s announcement, the CDC walked back its post , expressing appreciation for Kennedy’s efforts to clarify conflicting information from Pennsylvania officials about whether the two reported deaths were caused by measles.

Then, in an unusual move, on Aug. 30 , the CDC changed the death count on its measles dashboard from 2 to an asterisk, with a footnote stating that the National Center for Health Statistics currently has no death records from 2026 that indicate measles is the underlying cause.
No new evidence arrived in those two days that would explain the CDC’s new position.

HHS now says it is working with a national network of disease tracking experts on a standardized case definition for measles deaths. Standard case definitions exist for measles infections but not for measles deaths, for the simple reason that until recently, dying from measles in the U.S. was an extremely rare occurrence: Between 2001 and 2022 , the U.S. recorded roughly 4,000 cases and three deaths.

But writing a definition in the middle of a count – and applying it to a single state’s deaths – is a departure from protocol. Previously, during outbreaks in Texas and New Mexico in 2025, the CDC did count three measles-associated deaths while they were still being investigated. Declining to do so now is inconsistent and confusing , and breeds mistrust.

Unnamed officials told news outlets that CDC Director Erica Schwartz removed the deaths at Kennedy’s request , after CDC staff had accepted the state’s data. HHS disputes this, and Kennedy said in a post on X that the coroner’s finding – that the newborn boy’s death was caused by a ruptured spleen – vindicated federal caution .

A parent sifting through all this information has no way to gauge who is right. The usual shortcut – check the CDC numbers on the measles dashboard – now yields an asterisk leading to a footnote that contradicts statements from state officials, a county coroner and the agency’s own condolence post from 10 days earlier. There’s no neutral tiebreaker left, which means the decision falls back on which institution you already trusted most.
While that argument played out, a second rift was widening on a different track.

On Sept. 2, four physician groups – the American Academy of Pediatrics, the American Academy of Family Physicians, the American College of Obstetricians and Gynecologists, and the Infectious Diseases Society of America – issued their own vaccine recommendations for the fall respiratory season.

The pediatricians association had already split from the CDC’s childhood immunization schedule in 2025 , ending a 30-year practice of publishing one agreed-upon set of recommendations for families. What’s new is that three more societies have now joined this public health separatist movement, and that the split has extended to the shots most adults get.

On influenza, the physician groups’ advice matches the CDC’s: Everyone 6 months and older should get a flu vaccine. On COVID-19 they go further, recommending vaccination for children 6 to 23 months, whereas the CDC tells parents to consult a doctor.

For decades, the CDC has issued fall vaccine recommendations each year, offering a unified slate of federal advice for everyone across the U.S. to follow. Now, with the federal advisory committee that makes those recommendations sidelined and embroiled in a legal battle , the agency has issued no new federal vaccine guidance for this season. The four physician groups stepped forward to fill the gap.
Yet technically, the CDC’s previous seasonal recommendations – and its revised childhood immunization schedule – still stand, creating a confusing doubling of critical health guidance.

Measles is among the most contagious diseases known. Roughly 1 to 3 in 1,000 children who catch it die, and in 2025, 11% of cases required a hospital stay. A 2025 study put the average cost at roughly US$43,000 per case .

The national case count reached 3,134 on Sept. 4, the highest since 1991. As of the same date, Pennsylvania had recorded 624 cases – 91 in the previous week. More than 40% of Pennsylvania’s cases have been in Lancaster County.
Parents must now reconcile a recently revised federal immunization schedule, a set of physician-society recommendations that departs from it, a state count of two deaths and a national count of none.

Each of those positions has an institution behind it. None of them explains how it relates to the others – and that is what’s most damaging. Public trust doesn’t only collapse when officials lie. It erodes when people are handed different information that can’t be squared, or misleading information, and are left to sort it out alone.

articles.title: ‘The Uprising’ shows how medieval people weren’t so obedient after all
articles.author:
<name>Joëlle Rollo-Koster, Professor Emerita of Medieval History, University of Rhode Island</name>
      <foaf:homepage rdf:resource="https://theconversation.com/profiles/joelle-rollo-koster-1286920"/>
paras: For decades, I’ve been showing my medieval history students the “ autonomous collective ” scene from the 1975 film “ Monty Python and the Holy Grail .”

The clip is funny because it features two medieval peasants haranguing King Arthur while using the lexicon of a modern political Marxist. When Arthur explains that he was their king because the Lady of the Lake gave him Excalibur, one of the peasants objects: “Supreme executive power derives from a mandate from the masses, not from some farcical aquatic ceremony!”
It also subverts the assumption that medieval people were politically passive, with resistance to abuses of authority largely absent before the Renaissance and the Protestant Reformation.
But far from being an age of unquestioning obedience, the Middle Ages – the period from roughly 500 to 1500 – witnessed a remarkable number of popular revolts and collective political action.

Even if they didn’t speak in the language of Karl Marx, ordinary people back then held strong views about the working of political authority . And when they believed authorities had violated their obligations or lost their legitimacy, they routinely challenged rulers, bishops, tax collectors and urban elites.
In the 11th and 12th centuries, northern French peasants famously resisted carrying out the work or paying the money that they owed to the lords who controlled the land they farmed.
But perhaps the most well-known insurrection is the English Peasants’ Revolt of 1381 , the subject of the new film “ The Uprising ,” starring Andrew Garfield.

After the first wave of the Black Death in 1348 created a massive labor shortage in Europe, workers were better positioned to negotiate for higher wages and better conditions. Serfs – peasants bound to the land and subject to a lord’s authority – increasingly pushed back against oppressive feudal obligations.

But kings and lords resisted change. In 1351, England’s King Edward III decreed the Statute of Laborers , which froze wages, derailing any aspiration for social mobility among the peasant class. Resentment continued to build with recurring episodes of the plague.

Then, in 1381, Edward’s grandson and successor – 12-year-old King Richard II – instituted a one-time tax of 12 pence to raise funds for England’s ongoing war with France. Because the tax was charged per person rather than according to wealth, it placed a particularly heavy burden on poorer families.

The people had had enough: Crowds attacked tax collectors and eventually organized into a larger movement, burning houses, castles and the records that documented their obligations to their lords. They killed government officials before marching to London to confront the king.
The king met the rebels and pledged to abolish the poll tax and serfdom, while lowering the rent of agricultural land.
He later recanted those promises: His forces hunted down the rebels, quashing the uprising.

Insurrections like the English Peasants’ Revolt erupted, in part, because in cities across Europe, regular people had cultivated a strong tradition of collective action. There was broad membership in guilds , which were voluntary associations of merchants and craftsmen. Then there were neighborhood religious confraternities , which were akin to today’s religious mutual-aid societies. Together, they gave ordinary townspeople networks through which they could organize around shared interests and grievances.

Over in France, the Hundred Years’ War caused a breakdown in authority. People were increasingly being asked to pay taxes they couldn’t afford. Unpaid troops routinely raided the countryside, and the French military suffered a number of significant military defeats.

In 1358, the Jacques – a derogatory name for members of the lower French peasantry – razed noble estates and killed members of the aristocracy. They also joined forces with the Parisian bourgeoisie and the city’s chief political leader, Étienne Marcel, to fight for a greater voice in French government.

The rage underpinning the violence of what became known as the Jacquerie emerged from the fact that the same aristocracy that demanded so much of them could not fulfill their basic part of the bargain: protect them.

A little over a decade later, violence erupted in Florence, Italy. The city-state was an industrial juggernaut ruled by guilds, but their representatives all belonged to the urban elite. The lower classes of the textile industry weren’t represented by guilds and were largely disenfranchised. So the Ciompi – low-level woolworkers – demanded a role in the guild system. Those demands fell on deaf ears.

In June 1378, the Ciompi revolted and attacked government offices. Thanks to their efforts, they won participation in the guild system for four years, up until the city’s old powerful merchant elite dissolved their lower guilds.
Nor was the other main source of authority, the church, immune to attack.
When power vacuums emerged after the death of an abbot, bishop or even the pope, regular people routinely ransacked their property, taking with them a substantial amount of the dead’s movables.

“From various reports we are aware of the perverse and wholly detestable practice of certain people, who at the death of the bishop break in like enemies and rob his house, like thieves make off with his belongings, set fire to the homes on his estate, and with fierce and savage barbarity cut down his grape vines and orchards.”

Early Christian elections were initially open to entire congregations. Though these elections often gave the lion’s share of voting power to the wealthy and well-connected, there was the general understanding that everyone would play a role: “ vox populi, vox Dei ,” or “the voice of the people is the voice of God.”

However, by the end of the 13th century, the papacy had successfully established its authority over both ordinary people and secular rulers. On religious matters, there would no longer be public input. Instead, beginning in 1274, a conclave of cardinals elected the pope. The pope, sometimes still under the influence of higher lords, then nominated abbots and bishops.
The voice of the people had largely vanished. Nevertheless, they made themselves heard.
An April 1314 papal election in Carpentras, a small city in southeastern France, turned so violent that it delayed the naming of a new pope for nearly two years.

Deadlocked over the candidates, the cardinals dragged out the election for so long that frustrated locals attacked the episcopal palace where the conclave was being held. Cardinals and their staff fled and delayed until August 1316, when, under the protection of the French king’s forces, they nominated Pope John XXII .

Over 60 years later, in March 1378, Pope Gregory XI died. Amid threats from a crowd demanding an Italian pope, the cardinals elected Urban VI , an Italian, the following month. But over the ensuing months, the cardinals soured on Urban and declared their election invalid on the grounds that they had acted under duress. They elected a rival pope, triggering the Great Western Schism , during which two competing papal courts existed from 1378 to 1417.
Violence could also erupt for seemingly minor affronts.

In October 1367, Pope Urban V was in Viterbo, Italy. The pope and his court were French. The Viterbese took offense when papal court officials washed a little dog in their fountain of Piano di Scarano, which served as a source of drinking water. A confrontation followed, which escalated into a two-day uprising . The fountain was destroyed, and the pope and his cardinals were forced to take refuge in the Rocca Albornoz, the papal fortress.
Ideologies have evolved and technologies have advanced, but the fundamental struggle over who wields power, how authority earns legitimacy, and how compliance is enforced remains strikingly familiar.
The levers that leaders pull – taxation, welfare, infrastructure projects, propaganda, law enforcement – are largely the same, too.

Yet medieval folks understood that authority was a two-way street. When those in power didn’t hold up their end of the bargain, they were quick to resist, demand accountability and challenge authority.
In this sparring over power and consent, we can see, as one of Monty Python’s peasants put it, “the violence inherent in the system.”
