articles.title: The Lunch Lawyer
articles.author: Harry Cheadle
paras: If you work in the restaurant industry and your boss shorts your paycheck, you have limited options. You could quit, with or without sending your boss a nasty message, and start looking for a new gig. You could file a complaint with the Washington State Department of Labor and Industries or Seattle’s Office of Labor Standards, though the investigatory process typically takes months to complete. Or you could file a lawsuit, a choice that may lead you to the cramped, single-room office of Steven Toff.

Toff is the founder of Bread & Roses Law Group, a firm that specializes in employment law. He sues employers for discrimination of various kinds, for wage theft, and for denying workers mandatory breaks. Bread & Roses has taken on big employers like Boeing, Tesla, Whole Foods, and Thomson Reuters, but after Toff filed a class action lawsuit against the fine-dining restaurant Canlis in 2023, he became a go-to resource for restaurant workers in Seattle.

He’s sued restaurant owners, helped workers file complaints, and assisted employees looking to unionize. To him, it’s all an extension of his prior career as a labor organizer and union advocate; he wants to provide a way for workers in a precarious industry to claw back a few of their rights.

Restaurants, he says, are “where you see many of the problems I care most about: low wages, unstable schedules, tip dependency, informal (and often abusive) power structures, retaliation, and workers who often know something is wrong but have very little practical ability to enforce their rights alone.”

Anyone who’s ever worked in the service industry has likely run into routine violations of employment law. Toff himself remembers working at a pizzeria as a teenager in Tucson, Arizona. The owner habitually shaved hours off time cards to avoid paying them for work done after closing time; he also cornered a girl in the walk-in fridge to hit on her, Toff recalls. The experience “informs everything I do as an attorney,” he says.

Toff is tall and a bit scruffy for a lawyer, even one in the Pacific Northwest. He has more tattoos sprawling past the sleeves of his quarter-zip than the typical lawyer, too, traces of his time as a globe-trotting union advocate who’s lived in Brazil and Germany. Not that he’s left the bargaining table behind.

When employees at Renee Erickson’s critically acclaimed Sea Creatures group unionized last year, Toff agreed to aid contract negotiations for free. (This summer, the union won contracts at the Walrus and the Carpenter and at General Porpoise.) The union, which does not collect dues, would never have been able to afford representation, says United Creatures of the Sea organizer Ford Nickel. “Immediately upon meeting him,” Nickel says, “we realized that, like, this guy is a lawyer, but he is an organizer and supporter of workers and workers’ rights first.”

Before Toff was a lawyer or an organizer, he was a “punk-rock kid” from Tucson, getting his first sniff of left-wing politics through bands like Berkeley’s Crimpshrine. He moved to the Bay Area in the ’90s—ostensibly for college but really to play in bands, he says—and was further radicalized by the raw inequality he saw during the height of the dot-com boom.
“At the time, I had never seen that kind of homelessness,” he says. “I remember counting the number of people I saw living on the street, on the bus, on the way home.”

For Toff, the labor movement provided a way to address this sort of injustice. He majored in labor studies at San Francisco State and, in 2001, organized the Berkeley city recycling plant under the banner of the Industrial Workers of the World. After college, he worked for a number of unions throughout the West, including the American Federation of Labor and Congress of Industrial Organizations (AFL-CIO). He organized farm workers in California’s Central Valley, paper mill workers in Oregon, and airline employees in Phoenix, living in hotel rooms and visiting potential union members at home to explain the benefits of unionization. There were long days. And a lot of driving.

He became interested in international trade unionism and moved to Berlin for grad school, then wound up working for National Nurses United in New York. In hopes of getting a leadership position at a union, he attended law school at Northeastern University, then served as counsel for the New York State Nurses Association. During the pandemic, he and his family moved to Amsterdam to work for an international labor organization. They moved across the world again when his then-wife got a job in Seattle, a city Toff didn’t know at all.

When he arrived, Toff switched to private practice to normalize his working hours and spend more time with his kids. He began volunteering with the Emergency Workplace Organizing Committee, a Democratic Socialists of America–sponsored project that supports workers in difficult-to-organize workplaces with tiny workforces and high turnover. Unionizing tends to be a long and complicated process: Workers have to decide among themselves that they want to form a union—often by signing cards—then hold an election, then be formally recognized by management, then negotiate with management on a contract that will govern the new conditions of work. The entire process can drag on for years, especially if an employer stalls and fights the union at every step. As an example of how difficult this journey is, hundreds of Starbucks coffee shops have voted to unionize since 2021, but not a single one has completed a contract. These long timelines are partly why restaurant work is largely non-union—with so much staff turnover, organizing is borderline impossible, and the restaurant in question may close by the time a contract is signed.

Some of the electrical workers Toff talked to through the Emergency Workplace Organizing Committee were in similar straits; unionizing wasn’t really a viable way to address grievances with their bosses. But if their bosses were breaking the law, they didn’t need a union. They could sue.

“Steven sees angles and opportunities that a lot of people might not see, because he has such an open and creative mind,” says Carol Igoe, a labor advocate and lawyer who has known Toff for two decades and works with him at Bread & Roses.

The angle he saw in the electrical workers’ case was that in Washington State, nearly every employment law statute has “fee-shifting provisions.” That means that if a worker sues their employer and wins, the employer is on the hook for their legal bill. This is what makes Bread & Roses’ business model possible.

Toff mostly works on contingency, meaning his clients don’t pay him unless they win a settlement. The simplest way this works is that Toff sends an employer a demand letter informing them they owe a such-and-such amount in unpaid wages to his client, and that they also owe his fee, which might be $2,000 at that point. “So pay by Friday, or we will file a wage lien against your home in Bellevue and then file the lawsuit shortly thereafter, and we will win, and you will owe a shit-ton more, because you will owe the attorney’s fees, which at that point will not be $2,000, they will be $50,000,” Toff says. This can be a compelling threat.

Toff’s most famous suit was the class action against against Canlis, which he led while working at the local employment law firm Maloney O’Laughlin. Filed on behalf of all non-managers at the fine dining restaurant, it accused Canlis of requiring hourly workers to perform an initial unpaid “stage” shift in order to be hired and for not distributing all the money it collected via its “service charge” to the staff, as its menus claimed until mid-2022.

Evan Gallo, a former server and one of the named plaintiffs, says that in the run-up to the suit, some employees had circulated a petition asking for higher wages. Management declined this request, claiming they wanted to keep prices relatively low to be within reach of the non-super-rich, according to Gallo. Dissatisfied with that response, the workers looked into suing.

Gallo called several lawyers but “got the best vibe from Steven,” he says. “He’s very motivated to fight for the little guy.” Gallo helped sift through the timesheet records Canlis sent to the law firm to identify instances of workers not getting the service charge money they were due. This experience inspired Gallo to enroll in law school after the case concluded; he now works as Toff’s legal assistant. The suit, though, was divisive among the Canlis staff, Gallo says. Some workers regarded Canlis as a great place to work and disagreed with the decision to sue. (Another plaintiff says that they lost friends on the Canlis staff who sided with Canlis management.) After going through mediation, Canlis settled the lawsuit for $1.45 million in 2024. It did not admit any wrongdoing.

Toff launched Bread & Roses not long after that. He says the Canlis suit was “one of the cases that confirmed for me that there was real need, and real opportunity, for a workers’-rights practice focused on things like wage theft, including in industries like restaurants where violations can be widespread, but individual workers often do not have enough economic power to bring claims on their own.”

These lawsuits are sometimes an imperfect vehicle for workers’ grievances. The Canlis employees who came to Toff had complaints that went beyond the service charge language—it was just that the service charge issue provided a pathway to legal action.

Workers in the notoriously chaotic restaurant industry don’t really have many other options when they’re unhappy with management, as evidenced by how few restaurants in Seattle have unionized. (After Capitol Hill diner Glo’s unionized in 2023, workers voted to decertify the union months later after some staff turnover.) Organizers at the Sea Creatures restaurant group did succeed in securing contracts at the Walrus and the Carpenter and both locations of the General Porpoise doughnut chain after workers went on strike, but haven’t gotten a contract at the Capitol Hill steakhouse Jeffry’s.

Another obstacle restaurant unions face is that sometimes these businesses don’t make enough money to give employees substantially more wages or benefits. (Restaurants generally have profit margins under 9 percent, and a recent National Restaurant Association report found that 42 percent of restaurants weren’t profitable.) That’s what unionized workers at Sea Wolf Bakers learned last year when management opened their books during negotiations. Instead of an hourly wage increase, the two sides eventually agreed to let workers accept tips for the first time. Similarly, in the contracts negotiated by United Creatures of the Sea, unionized workers agreed to lower base pay rates and fewer benefits in exchange for the service charge model being scrapped in favor of receiving more tips.

Could there be some middle path between piecemeal lawsuits and high-effort union drives? Toff wonders if some restaurants could adopt simplified collective bargaining agreements that spell out basic pay and working conditions. “At a union restaurant in Seattle, there’s a 20 percent service charge and 100 percent goes to the workers,” Toff imagines, “and a sticker goes in the window that says, ‘This is a union restaurant.’” In progressive Seattle, where plenty of restaurant owners want to be seen treating their employees well, maybe something like that could work.

Canlis is far from the only Seattle restaurant to have been sued over its service charge language. Upscale diner chain Skillet and Tom Douglas’s restaurant group were targeted by similar lawsuits; like Canlis, both settled rather than going to trial. Some restaurant owners have privately complained to me that these suits punish them for technicalities. They argue that restaurants tend to shift to service charge models in order to address pay inequities caused by tipping; service charge money really does go to workers. But when a restaurant says that all of a service charge is distributed to workers, it has to meticulously track where every dollar goes or face legal liability. As a result, Seattle restaurants tend to adopt safer language. Canlis’s menu now reads, “A 20% service charge will be added to your final bill. 100% of this service charge is retained by Canlis.”

Toff thinks a service fee that doesn’t go to workers is “disingenuous,” and that in practice, restaurants are “just artificially deflating the cost of things on [their] menus.” He has a punk’s instinctive hatred of hypocrisy: Why can’t restaurants just work all of their costs into menu prices? If they won’t raise those prices out of fear of driving away customers but are really paying a living wage, why not just list the employees’ hourly pay on the receipt?

Given his background, it’s no surprise that Toff has no problem simply asking waiters how much they make. One time he did this and the server wouldn’t tell him. It eventually came out that the server was also the owner.
“And I said, ‘Oh, how much do the workers make?’” Toff says. “And he said, ‘I’d rather not answer that question.’”

articles.title: Slog AM: El Niño Is Getting Stronger, Sen. Patty Murray Is Going After Trump, and Trump’s Bribing Americans to Vote Republican
articles.author: Megan Seling
paras: Sen. Patty Murray’s pissed at Trump. In an effort to encourage “traditional” families , the Trump administration wants to pay married, stay-at-home parents with money from the Child Care and Development Fund, which was established in 1990 as a way to help parents—both single and married—pay for childcare so they could go back to work. “It’s not the 1950s in America,” said Murray in a statement. “Our government shouldn’t punish people for being single parents or choosing not to marry. … Raiding an underfunded program solely to score culture war points is not pro-family—it’s a wasteful grift that I will fight every step of the way.”

CM Bob Kettle’s (still) pissed at Mayor Wilson. Seattle City Council Member Bob Kettle wrote a public letter to Mayor Katie Wilson demanding to know why Wilson asked SPD Chief Shon Barnes to resign after the Bite of Seattle shooting. Barnes, who didn’t live in Seattle full-time and was hired by former Mayor Bruce Harrell, stepped down in July. CM Kettle’s letter does not acknowledge that hundreds of pages of internal messages suggest that, as Publicola reported , “the primary reason for the delay in information, as well as almost all of the delay in holding a press conference that night, was that SPD delayed the release of information repeatedly.” As Sutton would say: Let the mouse go .
Meanwhile, Mayor Wilson has launched a new task force aimed at improving Seattle’s economy and helping businesses “start, stay, and grow.” Very left-wing radical communist behavior, I know.

Trump, who famously survived 9/11 , spoke at the Republicans’ midterm convention yesterday and promised to pay every American $5,000 if the Republicans retain control of the House and Senate after November’s midterms. “It will be called the Trump Dividend,” he said. Where will the $1 trillion come from? JD Vance said tariffs, maybe? According to the Bipartisan Policy Center, the US has, as of August 20, earned about $189 billion from tariffs and excise taxes. You’re about 2.8 Jeff Bezoses short, my dudes. The AP reports that “the White House did not respond to a message seeking details.”

Houthi rebels in Yemen are advancing along the coast of the Red Sea. The Guardian reports that “By taking control of more of the Red Sea coast south of the port of Hodeidah, the Houthis’ aim is to put pressure on Saudi Arabia and the US to agree a deal that lifts the US blockade on Iranian oil tankers in the Gulf.” Gas isn’t gonna get cheaper anytime soon, y’all. Trump admitted yesterday that the war likely won’t end before November’s midterms. Ooooh, but just think about that juicy $5,000!!!!!!

In other the Future Is Fucked news , August was the hottest month ever recorded on Earth! El Niño is a factor, but experts say “our relentless burning of fossil fuels” is also a significant driver, especially because climate change exacerbates El Niño. One scientist added, “This summer has really been exceptional. We’ve seen records that existed for close to 100 years be broken, in the U.S. in particular.” U! S! A! U! S! A! U! S! A!

According to the World Meteorological Organization , there’s a near 100 percent likelihood El Niño will persist through February 2027, significantly altering “rainfall and temperature patterns worldwide and fuel extreme weather.” We are the world.

ICE activity at Boeing Field has “exploded,” according to Guadalupe Gonzalez, a member of La Resistencia. The Seattle Times reported that during one week in August, “authorities boarded roughly 400 people on ICE flights leaving Boeing Field.” It is believed they were taken to other facilities in the country, but, as the story points out, when people are “sent away on ICE planes, their loved ones and their lawyers are often left in the dark about what’s happening and why.” ICE’s contract with the GEO Group, which owns the Tacoma facility, ends in late October, though it’s unclear if the uptick of transfers is related. As KUOW reported in August, ICE is looking to buy “turn-key detention facilities in several states.” The Tacoma facility meets their requirements, but it’s unclear if they’re interested.
The Seahawks won their home opener yesterday , and the angsty little sister from Gossip Girl played songs with the surviving members of Soundgarden for some reason.

Here’s something to read later if you want to get very mad : This Mother Jones story about Jennifer Sey, the woman who founded XX-XY Athletics, details how Sey has gotten rich off the rise of anti-trans rhetoric among WNBA players and fans. Barf!

The race kicked off at Denny Way & Dexter Ave at 5:41pm as bus 8266 crossed Dexter Ave.
The bus immediately left almost everyone in the dust. After the first block, only a few runners kept up with the bus.

The bus picked up dozens of riders at the stops near Westlake Ave and Fairview Ave before barrelling towards the finish line, behind just three runners. Bus 8266 finished at 5:45pm, clocking in a total race time of 4 minutes for the half-mile race. Last year, the bus took 21 minutes.

articles.title: Metro Prevails in 'Race the L8' Rematch Thanks to New Bus Lanes
articles.author: Ryan Packer
paras: It was never going to be a fair race. Not with the new secret weapon in Metro's arsenal, a bright stretch of red paint extending all the way from Tilikum Place in Belltown to I-5. It's a bus lane that previous Seattle leaders had thought unthinkable, but at 5pm Tuesday more than 150 transit advocates showed up in South Lake Union to race a Route 8 bus up Denny Way, and got smoked by King County Metro.
The Urbanist's Fall Member Drive is in full swing! Support our work, read ad-free, and help us hit our goal for the member drive!

Well, most of them got smoked. Three runners, all of whom had clearly been getting their training days in, did manage to beat the 8 to Denny Way and Stewart Street by a few seconds, thanks in large part to extra bus dwell time to handle a sizable crowd of riders at Westlake Avenue.
Most of Tuesday's "racers" proceeded much more slowly than that first 8 coach did. Many even got to wave as another bus passed by on the way up the hill.

The event was a rematch, after last July's "Race the L8" saw cha-cha dancers, leapfroggers, and even someone driving a tiny car on the sidewalk ultimately beat a Route 8 coach up Denny Way. A whimsical illustration of the prior state of the infamous L8 bus, the event attracted significant media attention and shined a light on the issue in a brand new way.

The topic of the slow 8 was catapulted into the Seattle mayor's race, with then-candidate Katie Wilson (a regular Route 8 rider) making the trek up the hill with everyone else. The issue formed a clear contrast with former Mayor Bruce Harrell, whose administration was closed off to the idea of expanding bus lanes on Denny Way and reversed plans to add Third Avenue bus lanes in Belltown.

That attention turned into Mayor Wilson's very first executive order after taking office in January, spelling out a compact timeline to get red paint on the ground – this year. The road redesign included a reroute for traffic headed to I-5 onramps, which previously turned Denny Way into essentially a parking lot.

Things are very different 14 months later. With the new bus lane, Route 8 buses are traveling three times faster during the afternoon and evening peak period, according to preliminary data relayed by Wilson herself Tuesday. Riders traveling between Dexter Avenue and Fairview Avenue saved an average of 3.5 minutes – a huge amount multiplied across all of the route's riders – with the Route 8 recording its fastest travel times on Denny Way in at least seven years.

Racers saw even more dramatic bus acceleration in action Tuesday amid rush hour traffic. The bus took 21 minutes to complete the traffic-clogged half-mile race course back in 2025. On Tuesday, the bus took just four minutes – a staggering five times faster than the last race.

The reliability of the route has dramatically improved as well. Metro's trip times along the corridor varied by less than one minute last week, when it would oftentimes be more than 10 minutes without the bus lanes.

"Last summer, I joined many of you here to race the L8, and we saw firsthand what Route 8 riders have experienced for years and years and years: busses full of people stuck in traffic on one of the busiest corridors in our city," Wilson said in remarks to the crowd. "Riders and community advocates have been pushing for better Route 8 service for years, and I was proud to stand with them then. And I am very proud that we are here today celebrating real progress."

Making this project happen didn't just require a shift in mayoral priorities, it required a shift in departmental mindset. Last year, the assessment of a multi-block bus lane on eastbound Denny Way from inside the Seattle Department of Transportation (SDOT) was that the street grid couldn't handle such constriction of general-purpose traffic.

"This traffic congestion is expected to impact the ability of buses to access the bus lane and could result in backups in the bus lane itself," an SDOT blog post from last August stated. "Overall traffic would likely be significantly worse along Denny Way, with estimates showing general purpose travel times nearly doubling during peak travel times."
That traffic nightmare never came to pass.

"We were told that it was not possible to put a bus lane on Denny Way," Nick Sattele, who co-founded the Fix the L8 campaign in 2023, told racers Tuesday. "That the delay for drivers would be too high. It would destroy the bus, the transportation network. It would blow up traffic in South Lake Union. But we knew they were wrong because their studies didn't incorporate that drivers would take different routes, or that some drivers maybe would become transit riders as well."

Just a few weeks after the bus lanes were installed in mid-August, the traffic grid seems to be adapting to the new normal on Denny Way just fine. Travel times to Capitol Hill or I-5 by car are not dramatically up, and stretches of the road often look deserted during rush hour compared to past years. The traffic model was wrong, a fact that should have broad implications for transportation planning in Seattle way beyond the confines of Denny Way.

In addition to a faster bus, the project also resulted in safer sidewalks with fewer conflict points with car traffic. The former Yale Avenue intersection that used to clog the sidewalk and road with I-5 traffic has been curbed off to car traffic and is now a small pedestrian plaza where advocates congregated and mingled after the race.

Another remarkable aspect of the Denny Way project is the speed with which it was implemented. Bus lanes have traditionally taken years to be implemented in Seattle, subjected to substantial planning timelines or tied to larger capital projects. A northbound bus lane for the city's second-busiest bus, the Route 7 on Rainier Avenue, entered planning in 2022 and wasn't actually implemented until 2025.

In contrast, the Denny Way bus lane shows us how much that timeline can be compressed to prioritize transit riders sooner if the political support is there. Wilson and Councilmember Alexis Mercedes Rinck even helped paint bus lane markings themselves in a press event in late August .

"This is an incredibly encouraging start. Route 8 carries more than 7,000 riders every day and connects Downtown, South Lake Union, Capitol Hill, the Central District, and Mount Baker," Wilson said. "These are not just numbers. Saving time on the bus means more predictable trips to work, school appointments, and of course, home to spend time with your family. That is what reliable transit should do: make it easier for people to get where they need to go."
In fact, some people have moved to Seattle in part because of the attraction of the city's fast-improving transit, as race participants told The Urbanist on Tuesday.
"I just moved here too, and I'm from the south, where they hate public transit," Melissa said. "And it's f*ing awesome. It's so cool to have it."
Melissa raced with Aubrey and her dog Lola. Aubrey moved to Seattle after living all over the country, most recently in Olympia.

"As soon as I moved here and started taking transit, I immediately noticed how quick [it is]," Aubrey said. "I just think the dedicated bus lanes are amazing in general, and I do take the 8, and it avoids this whole cluster right here, which is great on the bus-only lane."
Taylor, who lives in Belltown and participated in the race, said used to avoid the 8 because it was a miserable experience to ride it, but that's changed seemingly overnight.

"Well, I have Ubered instead of taking the 8 because it's the only bus ride that I would get sick on from all the traffic," Taylor said. "I get carsick easily, and the 8 is the only bus that I consistently get carsick. It's the stop and start that would make me really dizzy."
Now the only thing holding back Route 8 is its frequency.

Earlier this month, Metro was able to boost frequency on the route during the afternoons on weekdays, bumping headways from 15 minutes to 12 minutes. But buses are still very full on rush hour, likely leading many riders to envy the frequency on the popular RapidRide G Line along Madison Street.

The good news is that more Route 8 trips could be on the way next year, if Seattle voters sign onto Wilson's plan to phase in 100,000 more annual bus trips with a beefed-up Seattle Transit Measure in November.

With the impossible now achieved on Denny Way to the benefit of thousands of daily transit riders, City leaders will have to decide whether to roll with the momentum created here... or be left in the dust.

articles.title: Kirkland Council Divides Over Affordable Housing Fees in Low-Density Zones
articles.author: Ryan Packer
paras: After spending most of the summer debating potential tweaks to new affordability requirements in the city's former single family neighborhoods, the Kirkland City Council last week opted to stay the course. The requirements, which will tack on a $15 per-square-foot fee to any units over 2,000 square feet in size, had been approved in mid-2025 and are set to take effect in January. But a proposal to raise the exemption threshold to 2,500 square feet proved surprisingly contentious, failing by one single vote on Tuesday after a deadlocked tie vote in June forced a revote.
The Urbanist's Fall Member Drive is in full swing! Support our work, read ad-free, and help us hit our goal for the member drive!

Mandates for builders to fork over a fee to fund affordable housing in low-density zones have been spreading across Seattle's suburbs in recent years. While often paired with an alternative option to construct those affordable units on site, such a move is often impractical, turning a so-called "inclusionary zoning" program into a new line item on a developer's expense sheet.
In nearby Redmond, a $30 per-square-foot fee has been phasing in since 2025 and will take full effect at the same time as Kirkland's $15 fee. In contrast, Redmond has no exemptions for smaller units.

The logic behind exempting smaller units from the new fee is straightforward. Kirkland, which approved one of the region's first " Missing Middle " housing laws in 2020 , has been seeing some densification in its lower density areas, but the city would like to see that pace pick up. Permits for 64 new cottage housing units were issued between May of 2024 and December of 2025, according to City records, compared to 104 new single-family homes.

The 2,000-square-foot exemption is intended to ensure that the city doesn't put a damper on those smaller, more affordable units. Even units slightly over the threshold would pay only on the portion of square footage above 2,000, keeping their overall fee relatively modest. However, councilmembers supporting the larger 2,500-square-foot exemption argued that setting the threshold too low could act as a disincentive for smaller housing types beyond cottage housing.

"When I think about middle housing, middle housing is cottages for sure, but it is also townhouses and smaller single-family homes. Data provided by the planning staff shows that the average-sized townhomes built in low-density zones is around 2,400 square feet, and the average size of townhomes that are built in medium-density zones are around again 2,400 to 2,500 square feet. And these are exactly the types of homes that I would like to incentivize in Kirkland," Councilmember Shilpa Prem said.

The 3-4 vote that left the 2025 plan in place saw Prem in the minority along with Amy Falcone and John Tymczyszyn and seemed to take several councilmembers by surprise. And the episode appears to signal deeper divisions on the council beyond this one issue – perhaps surprising given the results of last November's elections that saw election victories for all three incumbents on the ballot, along with Prem, who had been endorsed by outgoing Councilmember Penny Sweet. That was in spite of a considerable push to swing the council in a more anti-density direction.

The recommendation to stay the course came from City staff, who argued that raising the exemption "mainly benefits single-family homes which are not affordable to most community members," according to an August 18 staff report. Planning and Building Department Director Adam Weinstein pointed to the need to raise revenue for affordable housing, in order to make progress on a state mandate many cities are grappling with around planning for future residents at specific income levels.

"It's sort of our north star here," Weinstein said, showing councilmembers a chart of the city's growth targets. "It's really why we're considering this ordinance in the first place. It shows that we need housing in all income brackets, but the biggest need – 80% of the total need for about 10,444 units – is for housing that is affordable to households making less than 50% of the median income, and that's the housing that almost always requires some sort of public funding. And so, the generation of that funding is the primary intent of the ordinance that is in front of you tonight."
Kirkland staff project the fee will raise $3.3 million within 18 months of being implemented.

An amendment from Prem to raise Kirkland's per-square-foot fee to $20, an apparent bid at a compromise that would have recouped some of the lost revenue caused by raising the exemption, did pass on a 4-3 vote. But with the entire ordinance failing, that change ultimately became moot.

"Generally speaking, I'm not a huge fan of taxing housing to help us address the housing crisis. I just want to say that it seems a little counterintuitive, but I also want to acknowledge that we have very limited tools, right? And this is the situation we're in," Councilmember Amy Falcone said Tuesday. "This is not, in the grand scheme of things, the biggest issue and the biggest impact on housing affordability. It is something. It's a piece of the puzzle. We need lots of different pieces of the puzzle to be able to do this. But I do hope that in the future, like was mentioned, we have fewer restrictions on missing middle housing."

Inclusionary zoning programs across the U.S. – whether targeted at single-family neighborhoods or mixed-use districts – have come under increasing scrutiny as cities have been looking to jumpstart overall housing production. This summer, San Francisco slashed its affordable housing requirements from 15% of new units in a multifamily building to just 5%, with all buildings under 24 units fully exempted. Other cities like Cambridge, Massachusetts are considering following in San Francisco's footsteps.

In Seattle, builders in the city's Neighborhood Residential (NR) zones aren't required to pay any fees, in contrast with the city's denser districts where the Mandatory Housing Affordability program typically forces builders to set aside between 5% and 10% of units as affordable for 75 years or pay a hefty fee. Builders had been hoping to see temporary relief from those requirements citywide, but that has been proving to be easier said than done .

Kirkland Deputy Mayor Neal Black argued that expanding the mandate to fund affordable housing into the city's fringes is a move intended to balance out the requirements that the city imposes on builders in its growth centers.

"My objectives with this policy, are one to ensure the responsibilities assist in the production of affordable housing doesn't continue to fall disproportionately on multifamily housing," Deputy Mayor Neal Black said. "Number two, create more funding for affordable housing in Kirkland. Number three, foster construction of the greater mix of smaller homes Kirkland needs over the next 20 years. Four, ensure the Kirkland fees are less than, and no more complex than, our neighboring peer cities, and five, leave ourselves flexibility, legally speaking, to make favorable adjustments in the future."

Later this year, Kirkland will be considering potential code amendments that could make it easier to build middle housing throughout the city, but that work will not include another look at this new affordable housing fee. Any reassessment likely won't come until 2028 at the earliest.

"This was two years of effort with the community and with our planning department and our planning commission," Mayor Kelli Curtis said after Tuesday's ordinance failed. "Sometimes things are complicated and hard, and it takes us time."

articles.title: The Urbanist Fall Member Drive: Staffing Up to Expand Our Coverage
articles.author: Diego Batres
paras: 2026 has been an interesting year for The Urbanist. Our political endorsements are twice as popular as they were in 2025, we have a new website offering ad-free reading , and our coverage has grown to include the Eastside and cities outside Seattle more than ever before.
We're proud of our growing journalistic beats, but it also spreads our small team thin.

During this membership drive, we are asking you to help us fund the hiring of another employee. By helping us reach our goal of 100 new members by September 25th, you will put us in a position to sustainably grow our coverage, both geographically across the region and in the diversity of topics we cover. Members also read ad-free, as a treat!

With the Seattle media ecosystem in flux and local journalism on the decline, The Urbanist has been able to stay consistent and sustainable. We need your help to grow and expand our reporting on everything occurring in our region. A bigger team will also help us ramp up advocacy efforts to push for the urbanist future we all want.

If you would prefer to give to our 501(c)(3) arm, or take advantage of employer donation matching, you can direct donations to The Urbanist Fund , which supports The Urbanist’s (501c4) apolitical work.
Want to know what we’re using your donation for? You can peruse our 990 form , but the short answer is: paying staff.

The longer answer is that the vast majority of our expenses go towards paying our staff and freelancers. We pay business income tax despite being a nonprofit because of the advertisements on the website. Between taxes on the ads and the cut our third-party ad provider gets, we lose 1/3rd of revenue on ads – yet another reason we prefer donations!
Program expenses include technical expenses, such as website hosting expenses, and event program expenses, mostly venue rentals for panels and talks.

The single most important investment we make to bring you well-researched and well-reported news is qualified staff. That means reporters who know the region, understand urbanist policy, and have connections to the organizations and people who make policy decisions in our cities. All of this is to bring you, the reading public, the best reporting about urban issues in the region.
Support our writers by helping us hit our goal for this member drive and continuing to read and share our work!

Along with the member drive, we are finally completing the switch to the new website. If you were previously on our newsletter but not a donor, we created an account for you and subscribed you to the same newsletter you were on before. This is because we are ditching our old email sending service (Mailchimp), saving money and streamlining our workflow. All good things!

articles.title: Friday Roundtable: Race the L8 again… and lose?
articles.author: Nathan Dickey
paras: The L8 is not so late anymore since an eastbound traffic lane was converted to a bus lane in August. On Tuesday, September 8th , Fix the L8 is organizing another race against Metro’s bus Route 8 along Denny Way. Unlike the previous event , the group is expecting to lose as the buses bypass traffic via newly-painted eastbound bus lanes.

“Across multiple decades and several mayors, it’s been obvious that a bus lane is needed on Denny Way, and it only took a few months of Mayor Wilson’s leadership to get one” said Fix The L8 co-leader Jason Li. “This will transform the lives of the thousands of daily Route 8 riders while attracting countless more as it goes from being slower than hopscotching to being irresistibly good.”

Other traffic improvements, including closure of the Yale Street slip lane, have also helped speed up the bus. Although transit projects are often mired in years of design and debate, it’s abundantly clear that concerted effort and leadership can shorten this work to mere months. In this case, Mayor Katie Wilson requested accelerated design and construction of the transit prioritization project as her first executive order in January of this year. The improvements were announced in April and the project completed at the end of August .
Riders were quick to notice a vast improvement:

Despite the international media coverage focused on the impact this bus lane would have on drivers, travel times between Queen Anne Ave to Virginia St for cars has remained consistent. The chart below shows the estimated eastbound travel time for a car along the 1.1 mile segment of Denny way at the top of every hour since early July. The stripped blue section is the after the Yale St slip lane was closed in early August. The bus lanes were installed between August 21-23. Explore the full chart here .
The rematch race will begin at 5pm next Tuesday. Anyone interested is encouraged to RSVP to the event, here . The race will be followed by a celebratory gathering at The Pine Box in Capitol Hill.

The Fix the L8 campaign is also taking preorders of a tremendously-cute, limited-edition Route 8 plushie with first shipments expected to arrive in early October. The bus plushie (a busie!) is endorsed by STB as a perfect gift for the upcoming holiday season. Order yours here ! Proceeds go toward future campaigns for transit and street safety improvements.

articles.title: Cafe Lolo Is the Neighborhood Restaurant Every Neighborhood Deserves
articles.author: <name>Kat Thompson</name>
paras: If I were to describe the perfect neighborhood restaurant, Cafe Lolo would completely fit my definition. The food is comforting and nourishing, emphasizing local ingredients, which playfully come together in a way that feels both fresh and familiar. The space is draped in natural light that’s assisted by over a dozen lamps. The inviting dining room is covered in quirky Renaissance-inspired murals that don’t feel disruptive. There are to-go meal kits available for purchase, as well as local beers. It’s an atmosphere that invites you to unwind with a bottle of wine. Owners Leah Engel, Alex Halmi, and Brett Bankson are present, not only flitting about the room, but also cooking the dishes in the kitchen and laughing with customers. If I lived in the neighborhood, just off the main drag of Capitol Hill, it’s somewhere I’d want to return to over and over again.

Cafe Lolo has an extensive wine menu and many local beers, as well as bottles in the fridge you can pick up to-go. Although yes, the wine list — which includes just one glass from Washington, and more options from Oregon and Europe) — is worth perusing, the nonalcoholic tisanes are also made from seasonal ingredients. The strawberry rhubarb soda I had on my visit was effervescent and floral without an overpowering sweetness.

Like the rest of the menu, dessert will change pending seasons — but don’t skip it. My visit included a celebration of ripe, macerated strawberries over a semolina olive oil cake, which had a buttery crust and a tender interior crumb. There was also a scoop of rhubarb sorbet; light, sweet, and sharp.

It focuses on newer restaurants — typically opened or revamped significantly within the last six months or so — that are reshaping Seattle’s food scene for the better.

In July 2026, we added hot new “not a New York deli” Louie’s , Okonomiyaki Jiban-Ya , from the minds behind Ginger and Scallion and Secret Congee, and sleek Fremont tapas bar Balandra . As a reminder, if you go to a restaurant that has recently opened, be patient — the staff might not be firing on all cylinders yet, and there may be hiccups in the service or menu items that sell out.

articles.title: The Best Seafood Restaurants in Seattle
articles.author: <name>Mark DeJoy</name>
paras: Seattle is synonymous with seafood, and anyone who visits from out of town naturally wants to know where the city’s best seafood is. But that’s a tricky question. There are some self-described “seafood restaurants,” but fish and shellfish work their way into nearly every menu around Puget Sound. This includes oysters on the half shell at too many happy hours to count, crab and geoduck served as high-end delicacies, and sandwiches where freshly caught salmon or tuna is the star ingredient. A “best seafood in Seattle” map would pretty much just be a map of Seattle. So consider this a sampler platter of some of what the city has to offer across several different styles of cuisine and price point.
